item.title: Norway’s roads authority applied to test Tesla FSD in Brussels – but will give the EU no input
item.description:
The Norwegian Public Roads Administration (Statens vegvesen) applied to send three employees to Brussels on 10–12 November to test a Tesla with FSD, now called Tesla Assisted Driving. That is according to a travel application in the public records service eInnsyn, first reported by ITavisen. The applicant is Kenneth Sørensen, with Stein-Helge Mundal and Marianne Stølan Rostoft on the travel list. The test was to be run by Euro NCAP, which has fitted measuring equipment in the car. The aim was to learn more about driver monitoring during hands-off driving. The application does not say whether the trip went ahead.

Why it matters: It is good that the roads authority wants to try the system for itself. According to the application, the findings will be shared in an expert group on advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) and internally. The EU will get no input, however: Mundal considers that “train to have left the station”, he told ITavisen. He also denied that the trip had anything to do with TCMV, the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles. The committee meets on 15 December, but a vote has not been confirmed. His counterargument is that Norway has no vote there. The system is still not approved for ordinary owners in Norway.

Source: https://itavisen.no/2026/11/27/tesla-fsd-norge-vegvesenet-eu-ingen-innspill/

item.title: Norway’s roads authority will send the EU no input on Tesla Assisted Driving
item.description:
The Norwegian Public Roads Administration (Statens vegvesen) has no plans to give the EU any input on the approval of Tesla Assisted Driving (TAD), formerly FSD Supervised. Stein-Helge Mundal of the agency confirmed this to ITavisen. Nor does he know whether the agency will attend the next meeting. Asked why, he said he considered that “train to have left the station”. The wording of the documents to be voted on is now being discussed, and as an EEA country Norway has no vote. Its influence is “very limited”, he told ITavisen.

Why it matters: Mundal has a point: the decision is made in the EU. Even so, the passivity is striking. As recently as 17 November the agency set out three safety objections, including one against hands-off driving in built-up areas. Now it is not taking them to where the case will be decided, and it is unclear how they will be addressed, ITavisen writes. TCMV, the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles, meets on 15 December with the Tesla case on the agenda. A vote has not been confirmed. TAD is still not approved for ordinary owners in Norway.

Source: https://itavisen.no/2026/11/27/tesla-fsd-norge-vegvesenet-eu-ingen-innspill/

item.title: TCMV may vote on Tesla Assisted Driving on 15 December – the case is on the agenda
item.description:
Tesla Assisted Driving (TAD), formerly FSD Supervised, is on the agenda when the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles, TCMV, meets on Tuesday 15 December from 10.00 to 15.00. That is according to the draft agenda in the European Commission’s public register of committee meetings. Item 4, from 10.40 to 11.10, is a further examination of the Commission’s draft implementing decision authorising the Netherlands to grant EU type-approval for the system. The agenda says “with possible vote”. The tip came from FSD_DE and Rustavi on X.

Why it matters: A possible vote is not a promised yes. The committee may also simply discuss the case further, as it did on 6 October. A yes requires 15 of the 27 EU countries representing at least 65 per cent of the population. The Netherlands approved the system on 10 April, so eight months will have passed when the committee meets. That is slow, but an exemption from EU rules needs broad support. Nor does an EU yes apply automatically in Norway. Section 3-1 of the Norwegian vehicle regulations makes the EU type-approval rules Norwegian law, but Statens vegvesen must follow up under the EEA Agreement and has given no timeline. TAD is still not approved for ordinary owners in Norway.

Source: https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/comitology-register/screen/documents/119538/1

item.title: European Commission: TCMV meeting postponed to Tuesday 15 December – not 7 December
item.description:
The EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles, TCMV, will meet on Tuesday 15 December. A European Commission spokesperson told Reuters on Wednesday. The meeting was originally set for 1 December, according to the Dutch type-approval authority RDW. Earlier on Wednesday the Flemish transport ministry in Belgium said the meeting had been moved to Monday 7 December. We published that date here. The Commission has since said the meeting will instead be held on 15 December. Reuters journalist Marie Mannes updated the story at 11.46 Norwegian time. The Commission has given no reason for the postponement. The agenda has still not been published, so we still do not know whether the committee will vote on Tesla Assisted Driving (TAD), formerly FSD Supervised. The case concerns whether the Dutch approval under Article 39, the EU’s exemption procedure for new technology, should apply across the EU. In CIRCABC, the Commission’s document archive, the folder for the 120th meeting is still called “120th meeting on 1 December 2026”. The folder was empty when we checked it on Wednesday at 11.29. Statens vegvesen still writes that the next meeting is in December, but that it has not been decided whether there will be a vote. Its page was last updated on 29 October.

Why it matters: A yes in TCMV requires a qualified majority: at least 15 of the 27 EU countries, together representing at least 65 per cent of the EU population. Today 12 countries have approved TAD on their own. They have about 28.6 per cent of the population, according to our estimate based on Eurostat. That is a long way from a majority, even though owners in all 12 countries are already driving with the system. Norway has no vote in TCMV. As an EEA country we wait for the EU: Statens vegvesen will follow up under the EEA Agreement once the EU has decided. While owners in 12 EU countries use the system every day, Norway has chosen to wait for a meeting where it does not vote. The countdown on the front page now runs to 15 December. In the countdown model, the modelled dates move eight days later than when we used 7 December. That the committee votes and says yes on this day is still our assumption, not a decision. TAD is still not approved for ordinary owners in Norway.

Source: https://www.aol.com/articles/eu-postpones-discussion-approve-teslas-084108000.html

item.title: Italian owners are already driving with Tesla Assisted Driving – the rollout began on 21 November
item.description:
Tesla Assisted Driving (TAD), formerly FSD Supervised, has been rolled out to customers in Italy. The rollout began on Saturday 21 November, the day after Tesla Europe announced that the system had been approved. Italian YouTuber Giulio Autopilot said in a video the same day that his car had downloaded software version 2026.39.100 overnight. In the video he engages TAD in a Model 3 Performance and lets the car drive towards the Tesla centre in Bologna. The car stops at red lights, moves off on green and handles roundabouts while he supervises. The tracking service TeslaFi had registered the first five Italian cars on the version by 11.00 Norwegian time the same day, the website TeslAnt reports. On Monday morning TeslaFi shows 29 Italian cars on the version. The transport ministry MIT says in its press release that the vehicle authority Motorizzazione formally recognised the Dutch approval on 19 November, the day before the news broke. The subscription costs 99 euros a month. The driver remains responsible and must pay attention at all times.

Why it matters: Two days passed from Motorizzazione’s yes until the first Italian owners were driving with the system. That is exactly the median in the countries we follow. TAD is now in use by ordinary owners in all twelve EU countries that have approved the system. Italy is the first of the four most populous EU countries where owners are actually driving with it. The country has about 59 million inhabitants, more than ten times Norway’s population. While Italian owners are already driving with the system, Norwegian owners are still waiting. Statens vegvesen wants to wait for the EU and to see UN Regulation 171 met. The next chance of a yes in TCMV, the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles, is in December, but the meeting date has not been set. In Norway TAD is still not approved for ordinary owners.

Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nZ1ylm4Is7A

item.title: Tesla starts rolling out FSD v15 – still unclear for Europe and Norway
item.description:
Tesla has begun rolling out FSD (Supervised) v15. The company announced it itself on X on Saturday 21 November at 20.24 Norwegian time, together with a 47-second video. “FSD v15 now starting to roll out – upgrading every part of the end-to-end driving network,” Tesla writes. Tesla does not say which countries or which cars get the update first.

Earlier the same day, at 08.30, Tesla CEO Elon Musk wrote that v15 would reach many owners next month, in other words December. “FSD V15 goes to wide release next month. It will be something special.” Now Tesla says the start is under way. Neither Tesla nor Musk says whether the first wave is limited, or whether the wide release is still coming in December. Which software build it ships with is not yet known. Neither Teslascope nor Not a Tesla App showed a v15 build when we checked the sites on Saturday evening, 21 November. The newest consumer version there is still 2026.44.1, with FSD v14.3.13 for cars with HW4, also called AI4, and v14.3 Lite for older HW3 cars in North America. In the EU countries that have said yes, owners run a separate European branch: update 2026.39.100 with FSD version 14.2.2.7, according to Not a Tesla App.

Safety is what Tesla highlights first. The company writes that v15 handles safety-critical situations 25 times better. In the release notes posted by the account Tesla Super Intelligence (@TeslaSI), the figure is linked to an upgraded vision encoder shared by FSD, Robotaxi and Optimus and trained on millions of internet videos. The figure comes from Tesla, not from an independent test. FSD v15 also gets Tesla Reality View, a real-time visualisation that shows what FSD plans to do and lets you steer it. Navigation at the start and end of a trip now learns end to end from the fleet’s route choices, Tesla writes. Later v15 releases are to extend this to the whole route. You should notice better detection of signs, animals, road debris, potholes and standing water, and more natural speed handling in school zones and bad weather, according to Tesla. FSD can now slow down for speed cameras. A new Bike Rack Mode makes it possible to use FSD with a bike rack or similar equipment on the tow bar. FSD (Supervised) is still a Level 2 driver assistance system. The driver is responsible and must pay attention at all times.

Still from Tesla’s video when the company announced that FSD v15 is starting to roll out. Photo: Tesla.

Why it matters: The news shows how fast the system is improving – and how long Norwegian owners still have to wait. FSD Supervised, called Tesla Assisted Driving (TAD) in Europe, is still not approved for ordinary owners in Norway. Twelve of the 27 EU countries have already said yes, covering about 28.6 per cent of the EU population. The next chance of a yes in TCMV, the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles, is in December. The meeting date has not been set, and it is not known whether there will be a vote. The last meeting, on 6 October, ended without a vote. Statens vegvesen, the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, is in dialogue with Tesla but still has three reservations: hands off the wheel in built-up areas, the 10 per cent speed margin, and how Contextual Speed Adaptation, the system’s adjustment of speed to its surroundings, works when surrounding traffic drives faster than the limit. The agency has a point that the system must be safe on Norwegian roads. But RDW, the Dutch approval authority, has assessed the effect on road safety as marginally positive, according to the agency’s own page, and Tesla has changed the system several times at the authorities’ request. Our assessment is that v15 will probably have to be evaluated by RDW before it can be rolled out in Europe. That is an assessment, not information from Tesla or the authorities. Our countdown estimates that Norwegian owners will get the system at the earliest at the end of April 2027 and at the latest in August 2028. That is a model estimate with low certainty.

Source: https://x.com/Tesla/status/2124222447855743019

item.title: European Commission prepares the next step for Tesla Assisted Driving – in case the EU says yes
item.description:
The European Commission has prepared for what should happen after a possible EU yes to Tesla Assisted Driving (TAD), formerly FSD Supervised. That is clear from a slide from the 1 July meeting of the Commission’s Motor Vehicles Working Group (MVWG). A yellow box reads: “Preparation of Art. 40 (in case Art 39 of Tesla enters into force)”. The story is not new today. The slide is from July, and the minutes of the meeting are dated 15 September. The German X account TADWatcherDE reported on the documents on Saturday evening. We have retrieved them ourselves from CIRCABC, the Commission’s document archive. “In case” means contingency planning, not a promise. The presentation was produced by the Commission’s Joint Research Centre (JRC) and the Directorate-General for Internal Market and Industry (DG GROW). It carries a caveat that the views are preliminary and not the Commission’s final position. Article 40 of the EU type-approval regulation, (EU) 2018/858, sets out what happens after a yes. Once the Commission has granted an authorisation under Article 39, the exemption procedure for new technology, it must immediately start adapting the rules to the new technology. If the exemption concerns a UN regulation, the Commission must propose amendments to it. For TAD that is UN R171, the UN regulation on driver control assistance systems (DCAS). Once the rules have been amended, the restrictions in the authorisation fall away. In other words, the exemption becomes ordinary rules. The slide also shows the priorities the Commission has gathered for phase 3 of the DCAS work, dated June 2026. High priority goes to system-initiated manoeuvres, where the car itself initiates, for example, a lane change, on motorways and motorway-like roads with hands off. The same applies to system-initiated manoeuvres in cities with hands on the wheel. Hands-off driving in cities has low or no priority. In the same presentation, however, the Commission lists hands-off driving on city streets as one of the points it must look at under Article 40. Today R171 allows it only on motorways. The question the Commission asks is how it affects the driver’s attention.

The yellow box: preparation of Article 40 in case the Tesla approval under Article 39 enters into force. SIM means system-initiated manoeuvre, HOR is the request to put hands on the wheel, and wHOR means the system withholds that request, in effect close to hands-off. Slide: European Commission (JRC and DG GROW), MVWG meeting 1 July 2026.

Minutes of the 169th MVWG meeting, front page and item 8 on page 6. Source: European Commission, via CIRCABC. Yellow highlighting and crop: TADWatcherDE.

Why it matters: The slide shows that the Commission was planning for a yes as early as the summer. It is not a decision. First the EU countries in TCMV, the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles, must vote on whether the approval from RDW, the Dutch approval authority, should apply across the EU. The next chance is the December meeting. The date has not been set, and it is not known whether there will be a vote. In the minutes, the Netherlands describes how RDW assessed the system: data, studies and test reports, checks with simulation tools, on a test track and on public roads. It ended in a provisional approval because the system showed a level of safety as high as the UN regulation requires. The minutes refer to a Level 2 driver assistance system and do not name Tesla. The slide does. Switzerland asked how the system is monitored in use. The Netherlands replied that the results are shared with the countries that accept the approval. The road safety organisation ETSC (European Transport Safety Council) was concerned about the process. ETSC asked the MVWG subgroup on automated and connected vehicles to discuss the future of this type of driver assistance. The answer is in the same minutes: the approval is based on data, simulation and testing on track and road, and experience from use is shared with the countries. In the presentation the JRC also refers to its own test-track trials. There, the probability of a collision in critical situations was substantially lower with driver assistance than with manual driving. The trials concerned similar Level 2 systems, not TAD specifically. For Norway, Article 40 is good news in the long run. Regulation 2018/858 applies as Norwegian law through section 3-1 of the vehicle regulations. Statens vegvesen, the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, has said it will follow up under the EEA Agreement once the EU has decided. If the system becomes part of the ordinary EU rules, it is no longer an exemption Norway has to take a position on. That is our assessment. It is still food for thought that Brussels is planning step two while Norwegian owners are still waiting for step one. But the order follows the law: first the exemption, then permanent rules. TAD is still not approved for ordinary owners in Norway.

Source: https://circabc.europa.eu/rest/download/c97f5802-81f1-4ed5-bc15-648c2bfc83e0

item.title: Musk: FSD v15 goes to wide release in December – it may be the version Norway gets
item.description:
Elon Musk says FSD v15 will reach many owners in December. When Tesla Assisted Driving (TAD), formerly FSD Supervised, is one day approved in Norway, Norwegian owners may get v15 or an even newer version. That is our assessment. So far nothing has been confirmed about v15 in Europe. “FSD V15 goes to wide release next month. It will be something special,” the Tesla CEO wrote on X on Saturday 21 November at 08.30 Norwegian time. Musk did not say which countries or which cars it applies to. Tesla has given no date, so December is for now Musk’s own timetable. In the same post Musk writes that Tesla’s AI is trained without SFT and without a system prompt. SFT, supervised fine-tuning, means a finished AI model is adjusted afterwards with selected examples. According to Musk, that is more like “cutting hair with a chainsaw” than fine-tuning. A system prompt is a set of fixed instructions that steers a model; Musk calls it “silly”. He believes the model should behave sensibly on its own. A couple of hours earlier, at 06.02, the Tesla account Tesla Super Intelligence (@TeslaSI) had posted two letters: “XV”, the Roman numeral for 15. Ashok Elluswamy, who leads Tesla’s AI work according to his own X profile, shared the post with the same text. Tesla’s main account shared it too, with the text “What if we are just driving in a video game”. None of the posts mentions FSD in words, but it is natural to read “XV” as a hint about v15. In North America the newest version is now FSD (Supervised) v14.3.13 for cars with HW4 and v14.3 Lite for older HW3 cars. Both come with software update 2026.44.1, released on 17 November, according to the website Not a Tesla App. In the EU countries that have said yes, owners run a separate European branch. Update 2026.39.100 from 11 November has FSD version 14.2.2.7, according to Not a Tesla App. It includes the changes that RDW, the Dutch approval authority, approved on 3 November: the new name and a speed margin of at most 10 per cent over the limit. The European branch is therefore behind the North American one. Musk has more plans for December. On Monday 16 November he told an Uber driver in Austin, Texas, that trials in which owners let their own cars drive as robotaxis could start next month if all goes well. That says nothing about Europe.

Why it matters: The approval in Europe does not cover FSD in general, but the system RDW has assessed. When Tesla changes it, the company asks RDW to assess the changes. That has happened twice in November. On Monday 16 November RDW approved a new round as an extension of the existing type-approval and also mentioned “general improvements in the model”. Neither Tesla nor RDW has said whether v15 is coming to Europe, when that would happen, or whether the new version must go through the same process. Our assessment is that v15 will probably have to be evaluated by RDW before it can be rolled out here. That is an assessment, not information from Tesla or the authorities. In Norway TAD is still not approved for ordinary owners. Statens vegvesen, the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, writes that it will follow up under the EEA Agreement once the EU has decided. The next chance of a yes in TCMV, the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles, is in December. The meeting date has not been set, and it has not been decided whether there will be a vote. Twelve of the 27 EU countries have already said yes. Our countdown estimates that Norwegian owners will get the system at the earliest at the end of April 2027 and at the latest in August 2028. That is a model estimate with low certainty. If it takes that long, it is quite possible that v15 or an even newer version will be the first one Norwegian owners get to try. That assumes Tesla gets the version approved in Europe first, and nobody yet knows how quickly that will happen. The agency has a point that the system must be safe on Norwegian roads. But RDW has assessed the effect on road safety as marginally positive, according to the agency’s own page, and Tesla has changed the system several times at the authorities’ request. The driver remains responsible and must pay attention at all times. While Norway waits for the EU, Tesla keeps developing the software.

Source: https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2124042864891982292

item.title: Italy has approved Tesla Assisted Driving – the first large EU country to say yes
item.description:
Italy has approved Tesla Assisted Driving (TAD), formerly FSD Supervised, according to Tesla. “Now approved in Italy,” Tesla Europe wrote on X on Friday 20 November at 11.21 Norwegian time. The rollout begins soon, the post says. It opens with “Mamma, butta la pasta”, literally “Mum, put the pasta on”. Later on Friday, Deputy Prime Minister and Transport Minister Matteo Salvini confirmed on X that the transport ministry, Ministero delle Infrastrutture e dei Trasporti (MIT), has granted a provisional national approval after a thorough technical assessment. Italy is therefore not waiting for the EU. The subscription costs 99 euros a month, Corriere della Sera and the news agency AFP report. Tesla has given no rollout date. The application had been with MIT since July, when Tesla asked for the Dutch approval to apply in Italy as well. The Italian website Teslers.it reported this on 13 July, after a director-general at the ministry had confirmed the application to a Tesla owner. Salvini said on 29 October that Italy supports a swift EU approval. The driver remains responsible and must pay attention at all times.

Why it matters: Italy has almost 59 million inhabitants, about 13 per cent of the EU population. It is the first of the four most populous EU countries to say yes. Germany, France and Spain are waiting for the EU. The largest country to have said yes before Italy was the Netherlands, with 18 million. Counting Italy, twelve of the 27 EU countries have approved the system. They have about 28.6 per cent of the EU population, according to our estimate based on Eurostat figures. The share almost doubled in a single day. A yes in TCMV, the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles, requires 15 countries and 65 per cent of the population, and there Italy’s vote carries weight. The next chance is in December, but the meeting date has not been set. Norway is still waiting. Statens vegvesen, the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, is not considering any earlier introduction as long as the system does not meet UN Regulation 171, and is waiting for the EU. The agency has a point that the system must be safe on Norwegian roads. But more and more authorities have assessed the same system and said yes, and now one of the EU’s largest countries is among them. In Norway TAD is still not approved for ordinary owners.

Source: https://x.com/teslaeurope/status/2123723334542332026

item.title: Hungary won’t wait for the EU – the government will test Tesla Assisted Driving itself
item.description:
Hungary will test Tesla Assisted Driving (TAD), formerly FSD Supervised, on its own roads without waiting for the EU. Zoltán Tanács, Minister for Science and Technology, announced this in a video on Facebook on Sunday 15 November. An official, government-run test programme is to show whether the system drives safely and follows Hungarian traffic rules. The decision came after a meeting with Dávid Vitézy, who heads the Ministry of Transport and Investment, and his experts. The start date is not known. The test programme is not an approval, and Hungarian owners cannot use the system yet. Over the summer, the line in Budapest was that Hungary would wait for the EU vote.

Why it matters: Hungary is yet another country moving from waiting for the EU to acting on its own. The Czech Republic and Croatia also said at first that they would wait, and said yes a few weeks or months later. Our countdown therefore moves Hungary from May 2027 to 3 January 2027. That is a model estimate with low certainty, not a date from the Hungarian authorities. Eleven EU countries have already recognised the Dutch approval, and RDW, the Dutch approval authority, has assessed the effect on road safety as marginally positive. Norway is standing still. Statens vegvesen, the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, is not considering any earlier introduction as long as the system does not meet UN Regulation 171, and is waiting for the EU. The next chance of a yes in TCMV, the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles, is in December, but the meeting date has not been set. In Norway TAD is still not approved for ordinary owners.

item.title: Norway’s roads authority won’t follow Finland – three points are holding back Tesla Assisted Driving
item.description:
Statens vegvesen, the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, will not fast-track Tesla Assisted Driving (TAD), formerly FSD Supervised, even though Finland said yes on 10 November. Senior adviser Stein-Helge Mundal told ITavisen on Tuesday evening. He points to three unresolved issues. The agency still has questions about hands-off driving in built-up areas with many pedestrians and cyclists. It is also sceptical about letting the driver set a speed margin of 10 per cent above the limit. And it wants to know more about how the Contextual Speed Adaptation feature affects speed when surrounding traffic drives faster than allowed. According to ITavisen, Mundal also notes that a far larger share of Tesla cars in Norway than in Finland can use the system, so a Norwegian yes could have much greater consequences. Finland’s argument about letting owners get to know the system before the worst of winter does not sway him. “Our job is to make sure the system is safe to use on our roads, whatever the season,” he says. Tesla gets credit for the name change, which according to Mundal makes it clearer that this is driver assistance and not self-driving.

Why it matters: What is new is that the roads authority answers directly why Norway is not doing what Finland did. The Norwegian line still stands. The agency’s own website, last updated on 29 October, says Norway is not considering any earlier introduction as long as UN Regulation 171 is not met. The argument about many compatible cars can also be turned around: more cars means more Norwegian owners missing out on a system that Finland’s Traficom believes has great potential to reduce accidents caused by human error. RDW, the Dutch approval authority, has assessed the effect on road safety as marginally positive, according to the agency’s own page. Tesla has also complied with several demands. The speed margin has been cut from 50 to 10 per cent, and on 16 November RDW approved an update that makes the speed settings clearer to the driver. Mundal has a point that the driver must know the system’s limits. The responsibility always lies with the driver. The decision lies with the EU in any case. Once TCMV, the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles, has decided, the agency will follow up under the EEA Agreement. The next chance of a yes is in December, but the meeting date has not been set. Eleven EU countries have said yes. In Norway TAD is still not approved for ordinary owners.

Source: https://itavisen.no/2026/11/17/tesla-fsd-norge-vegvesenet-finland-godkjenning/

item.title: RDW approves a new Tesla Assisted Driving update – hands on the wheel above 130 km/h
item.description:
The Dutch approval authority RDW has approved yet another update of Tesla Assisted Driving (TAD), formerly FSD Supervised. RDW says so in a news release on 16 November, barely two weeks after the previous round. The system warns earlier when the driver is not paying attention, and it can issue a “full strike”, a warning that counts in full, if the driver is inattentive in the middle of a manoeuvre. Above 130 km/h the driver must keep their hands on the wheel. The speed display also becomes clearer. When the system uses the variable speed feature Contextual Max Speed, the driver is notified, and the speed indicator pulses when the system avoids slowing down. If the driver wants a higher top speed than the system suggests, it must be confirmed with the scroll wheel on the steering wheel. If the car is actually driving faster, the speed limit sign on the screen flashes red, and the current limit is shown next to the speed. On top of this come general improvements that RDW does not describe further. The update applies to cars with hardware version 4.0 (HW4) or newer and arrives over the air. Tesla decides when.

Why it matters: RDW tested the changes both on a test track and on ordinary roads and found no negative or unintended effects. item.title: RDW approves changes to Tesla Assisted Driving – the speed margin is cut to 10 per cent
item.description:
The Dutch approval authority RDW has assessed and approved several changes to FSD Supervised, called Tesla Assisted Driving (TAD) in Europe. RDW says so in a news release on 3 November. The new name must appear on the car’s screen, in the owner’s manual and in all other information to the driver. According to RDW, the name change does not alter how the system works. It is still a driver assistance system, and the driver is still responsible for driving. The biggest change concerns the speed margin, meaning how many per cent the system may deviate from the speed limit when needed for safety and traffic flow. The driver could previously set it at up to 50 per cent. Now the cap is 10 per cent. When the car is started, the margin is set to zero, and other speed-related functions are switched off by default. The changes apply to cars with hardware version 4.0 (HW4) or newer and arrive as an over-the-air software update from Tesla. RDW gives no date for when the update will arrive.

Why it matters: It was Tesla itself that asked RDW to assess the changes. RDW found no negative or unintended effects and has incorporated the changes into the existing type-approval. It continues to apply on the same conditions, and RDW has informed the nine countries that have recognised the Dutch approval. The number of countries is still ten. The process in the Netherlands is moving, and now it is up to the EU and Norway to follow. Statens vegvesen, the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, wants UN Regulation 171 met without exception. RDW does not comment on the handling in TCMV, where the talks are confidential. Norway has no vote there, and FSD Supervised is still not approved for ordinary owners in Norway.

item.title: Tesla owner complains about the roads authority’s FSD official – Mundal responds

The background is an email exchange from August. The owner argued that FSD Supervised, called Tesla Assisted Driving in Europe, can save lives, and that the Norwegian wait leads to unnecessary deaths. In the same reply he referred to the NRK documentary “Kollisjonskurs – Elon Musk og Tesla-eksperimentet” (Collision Course – Elon Musk and the Tesla experiment). Why it matters: The case shows how firmly the Norwegian line holds. SVV wants UN Regulation 171 met without exception, while ten countries have recognised the Dutch approval. item.title: Norway’s roads authority in dialogue with Tesla – and “positive about new vehicle technology”
item.description:
Statens vegvesen (SVV), the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, has rewritten its information page on advanced driver assistance systems. The page is marked “Last updated: 29 October 2026”. SVV now calls the system “Tesla Assistert Kjøring (tidligere Tesla FSD)”, Norwegian for Tesla Assisted Driving (formerly Tesla FSD). It is the same system we refer to as FSD Supervised, and which is called Tesla Assisted Driving in Europe. The biggest change is the tone. In October SVV wrote that it had no process with Tesla. Now it says SVV “is in dialogue with Tesla about updates and incident reporting”. The agency also writes that “Norwegian authorities are positive about new vehicle technology”, and that the current rules do not prevent the use of navigation, speed and steering functions that do not involve taking the hands off the wheel. According to SVV, Tesla has adapted the system after dialogue with authorities in several countries: the name has been changed, the marketing of the safety benefit has been toned down, and Tesla has dropped the exemption on maximum lateral acceleration. SVV expects Tesla also to adjust the system so it follows speed limits better. Tesla Norway has been allowed to use three modified cars for internal testing in Norway. SVV still has concerns: the driver can take their hands off the wheel outside motorways, the system can more easily break the speed limit, the driver may rely on it too much, and the driver monitoring is little tested. The same page says that RDW, the Dutch approval authority, has assessed the effect on road safety as marginally positive. Customer demos are still not allowed. SVV considers the customer information material misleading because it does not say that this is a driver assistance system, and has not yet received new material. The objection, in other words, concerns the material for customers. The same page shows that Tesla has already changed the name and toned down the marketing of the safety benefit after dialogue with the authorities, and that RDW has assessed the effect on road safety as marginally positive. Even so, it is not a Norwegian approval. ITavisen covered the same update on 30 October and wrote that the answer “will disappoint”, since the system is still not approved for Norwegian customers, but the same SVV page also shows that the agency is now in dialogue with Tesla.

Why it matters: The tone is clearly more positive than in October, but this is no Norwegian approval. SVV is still not considering introducing the system in Norway before it meets the UN regulation R171, even though several EU countries have said yes nationally. The decision waits for the EU. According to SVV, the next meeting of TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles) is in December 2026, but it has not been decided whether there will be a vote, and the text that may be voted on has not been settled. Once the EU has decided, SVV will follow its obligations under the EEA Agreement. The sentence saying Norway can oppose the introduction is gone from the page. Until then FSD Supervised is not approved for ordinary owners in Norway, while ten EU countries, Denmark among them, have said yes.

Source: https://www.vegvesen.no/fag/trafikk/its-portalen/its-i-statens-vegvesen/metr/forerstottesystemer/

item.title: New Tesla figures: nine times as far between major collisions with FSD Supervised
item.description:
Tesla has published new safety figures for FSD Supervised, called Tesla Assisted Driving in Europe. According to the figures, as cited by Tesla writer Sawyer Merritt on X on 27 October at 04.37, Teslas with the system engaged drove an average of 6,006,200 miles, about 9.7 million kilometres, between each major collision. That is 9.1 times as far as Tesla’s estimate for the US average, 660,164 miles. Teslas driven manually with the active safety systems on reached 2,031,221 miles, and without them 845,915 miles. FSD thus comes out with 3.0 times the distance of manual driving in the same cars and 7.1 times that of manual driving without active safety systems. The basis is 9.48 billion miles with FSD and 1,579 major collisions over the past twelve months. According to Merritt, the figures cover North America. By a major collision Tesla means that airbags or other deployable restraints were triggered, under the US definition in 49 CFR § 563.5. According to the methodology page on tesla.com, a collision counts as FSD driving if the system was engaged at any point in the five seconds before it. Tesla does not assess who was at fault. The figures are Tesla’s own, and there are caveats: much FSD driving happens on motorways, Tesla cars are newer than the average car, and drivers choose when the system is on. Tesla itself writes that the comparison with the US average rests on assumptions. The cleanest comparison is therefore with Teslas with the same active safety systems, and there the distance between major collisions is three times as long with FSD engaged. The driver must still pay attention at all times and is responsible.

Why it matters: According to Merritt, the figures cover North America and say nothing directly about European roads. But this is the kind of data the EU and Norway must weigh when FSD Supervised is dealt with in TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles). The system is approved in ten EU countries, and the next chance of an EU yes is expected in December 2026, but the meeting date has not been set. Transport Minister Kamzy Gunaratnam told the Storting, Norway’s parliament, on 16 October that Norway is awaiting the EU’s decision, and FSD Supervised is not yet approved for ordinary owners here.

item.title: EU minutes from the June meeting: 40 million kilometres with FSD Supervised – and speed on average below the limit
item.description:
The European Commission has published the minutes of the 30 June meeting of TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles). They were published on 16 October in the comitology register, the Commission’s public archive of committee work. The minutes show what the Netherlands presented on FSD Supervised, now called Tesla Assisted Driving in Europe. By the time of the meeting, RDW, the Dutch approval authority, had recorded 40 million kilometres driven with the system engaged. When the system adapts its speed to surrounding traffic, the data show it is on average 4.4 km/h below the speed limit the car has registered. The Netherlands also defended the speed margin the driver can set above the limit. The system is trained to drive like the best drivers, and the margin means the driver does not have to override with the pedal so often. Several member states pointed out that such systems can make roads safer and speeds lower. Others asked about driving in bad weather and about the fixed speed margin. The Commission concluded that the timetable depends on whether the Commission and the member states are satisfied with the answers from the Netherlands. Statens vegvesen (SVV), the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, attended for Norway, without a vote. Updated 21 October: the figure of 4.4 km/h below the speed limit contrasts with Transport Minister Kamzy Gunaratnam of the Labour Party (Ap). In her answer to written parliamentary question 15:116 on 16 October, she justified the Norwegian wait partly by saying the system “can actually break speed limits”. An average below the limit does not mean the car never speeds, but the minutes show that the system on average stays below the limit when it adapts its speed to traffic. The figures are the Netherlands’ own, as reported in the minutes.

Why it matters: The minutes are the Commission’s own summary of what the Netherlands presented at the June meeting. The figures support the line taken by the nine EU countries that have already said yes: the system has been used over very long distances, and when it adapts to traffic it keeps its speed below the limit on average. The speed margin is still the main point of contention. On that point the German transport ministry BMV agreed with Tesla in September on a cap of ten per cent above the limit, and Germany will back that line in the EU. Norway sent written questions before the June meeting, but no questions or comments for the meeting on 6 October, according to SVV. The next chance of an EU yes is expected in December 2026, but the meeting date has not been set. In Norway FSD Supervised is not yet approved for ordinary owners.

item.title: Minister answers the Christian Democrats: Norway waits for the EU, even though SVV says the system drives well
item.description:
Norway will not approve Tesla’s driver assistance system on its own. Transport Minister Kamzy Gunaratnam of the Labour Party (Ap) writes so in her answer to the written question from member of parliament Jørgen H. Kristiansen of the Christian Democrats (KrF), document no. 15:116. The answer came on 16 October. The minister believes road safety is best served by Norway “awaiting the EU’s decision”. If the EU says yes, Norway will follow “our obligations under the EEA Agreement”. At the same time she writes that she is “positive about new vehicle technology”. Statens vegvesen (SVV), the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, gives the system a good report: according to the answer, it appears to handle normal traffic situations “in a good way”. The minister also writes that Tesla has toned down its marketing and renamed the system. On Tesla’s Norwegian pages it is now called “Tesla Assistert Kjøring”. She gives two reasons for the wait. It has been shown that the system “can actually break speed limits”. And it is uncertain whether the driver is ready to take over immediately when the system fails. The answer also states that SVV gave input on Norway’s behalf to the meeting of the EU vehicle committee on 30 June. The input concerned, among other things, speed limits and the gap between the marketing and the owner’s manual.

Why it matters: The conclusion is the same as before: Norway waits for the EU. Nine EU countries have not waited. The Danish Road Traffic Authority, Færdselsstyrelsen, accepted the provisional approval from RDW, the Dutch approval authority, on 9 June after reviewing the technical documentation. The authority believes the system makes a positive contribution to road safety. Slovakia said yes on 16 October, the same day the minister replied. The Netherlands, Lithuania, Estonia, Belgium, Slovenia, the Czech Republic and Croatia have also accepted the system. Speed limits have also been addressed. In September the German transport ministry BMV agreed with Tesla that the system may drive at most ten per cent above the speed limit, and Germany will back that line in the EU. BMV also writes that the system has so far shown high performance, especially in city traffic. Norway has no vote in TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles). The next chance of an EU yes is December 2026. Until then FSD Supervised is not approved for ordinary owners in Norway.

Source: https://www.stortinget.no/no/Saker-og-publikasjoner/Sporsmal/Skriftlige-sporsmal-og-svar/Skriftlig-sporsmal/?qnid=127642

item.title: Slovakia says yes: FSD Supervised approved in a ninth EU country – Norway still waits
item.description:
Slovakia has approved Tesla’s driver assistance system FSD Supervised, now called Tesla Assisted Driving in Europe. The Slovak transport ministry writes on 16 October that it has officially recognised the provisional type-approval. RDW, the Dutch approval authority, granted it in April under Article 39, the EU’s exemption procedure for new technology in framework regulation 2018/858. Other countries can accept the approval nationally, and Slovakia has now done so. That makes nine EU countries that have said yes, with about 13.9 per cent of the EU population. Transport Minister Jozef Ráž says in the press release that road safety is very important, and that the ministry is happy to support new solutions that make roads safer. He stresses that the driver still bears full responsibility. Ráž promised the recognition on 7 October, nine days earlier. Tesla has given no date for the rollout in Slovakia.

Why it matters: Yet another EU country takes the shortcut while the EU vote keeps everyone waiting. Nine of 27 is a third of the EU countries, but still far from the thresholds for a yes in TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles): 15 countries and 65 per cent of the population. The next chance is December 2026. Statens vegvesen (SVV), the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, is not considering any Norwegian introduction before then, as long as the system does not meet UN Reg. 171 (the UN regulation on driver assistance systems). In Norway FSD Supervised is not yet approved for ordinary owners.

Source: https://www.mindop.sk/media/tlacove-spravy/detail/slovensko-umoznilo-ciastocne-autonomne-riadenie-aut

item.title: Tesla unveiled the new Roadster overnight – it drives upside down and can fly
item.description:
Tesla unveiled the new Roadster overnight into 16 October. The broadcast began at around 02.55 Norwegian time from SpaceX’s test facility in McGregor, Texas, according to Tesla, Reuters and Wired. The car drove up a vertical ramp using a fan-powered suction system, flipped in mid-air using compressed-air thrusters and flew over the rest of the Tesla line-up, The Verge writes. Tesla lists three versions on its website: Performance, a two-seater for ordinary roads; Thrust, a two-seater with rear thrusters; and Rocket, a single-seater with thrusters all round. According to The Verge, Tesla promises 0–60 mph (just under 100 km/h) in under 1.6 seconds for Performance, under 0.9 seconds for Thrust and under 0.59 seconds for Rocket. During the event Tesla gave 0.81 seconds. Musk says the top speed is over 230 mph (about 370 km/h) and that production starts in 2028. No price was given. For now only Performance can be reserved. The Rocket version is not approved for public roads, Tesla says.

Why it matters: Tesla calls the Roadster “the best of the last human-driven cars”. In other words, Tesla itself sees the future in cars that get more help with driving. We have found nothing about FSD Supervised or Tesla Assistert Kjøring (Tesla Assisted Driving) in the Roadster, either in Tesla’s posts or on its website. In Norway FSD Supervised is not yet approved for ordinary owners.

Source: https://www.tesla.com/roadster

item.title: Norway’s roads authority praises Tesla’s name change – “Full Self-Driving” is gone from the Norwegian website
item.description:
Statens vegvesen (SVV), the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, welcomes Tesla dropping the name “Full Self-Driving” (FSD). Since 8 October the features have been called “Tesla Assistert kjøring” (Tesla Assisted Driving) on Tesla’s Norwegian website. “It is positive that Tesla is now clearer in its wording. The most important thing for us is that users understand that this is still a driver assistance system. The driver is responsible for driving at all times and must follow the traffic and be ready to take control immediately,” SVV chief engineer Stein-Helge Mundal writes to Tek.no. According to Tesla, the name change applies across Europe, and the features work as before. The company has discussed the name with European and local authorities. The Norwegian subscription package is now called “Tesla Assistert kjøring grunnleggende” (basic) and costs 1,090 kroner a month. The more advanced software is still not available in Norway.

Why it matters: The name was one of the obstacles at home. In an update on 13 May, SVV called Tesla’s information material for customer demos misleading because it did not say the system is driver assistance. The agency would not allow demos until it was changed, and on 3 July it had still not received new material. Now “assisted driving” is in the name itself, and SVV gives praise. Eight EU countries have allowed the system, and Slovakia is expected to become the ninth, according to the news agency Reuters. Reuters has also reported on seven road safety researchers who believe Tesla’s European safety study does not document its claims. RDW, the Dutch approval authority, rejects the criticism and says the assessment was independent and thorough. An EU vote could come in December. In Norway the system is not yet approved for ordinary owners.

Source: https://www.tek.no/nyheter/nyhet/i/vl9npm/tesla-vraker-full-selvkjoering-navnet

item.title: The French get to test-drive FSD Supervised at the Paris motor show – Norwegians do not
item.description:
Tesla is letting visitors at the Mondial de l’Auto motor show in Paris try FSD Supervised, now called “Tesla Assisted Driving” in Europe. The show is open to the public on 13–18 October. Six Model 3s with the system are ready at the show’s test centre for self-driving cars, the “Autonomous Lab”, at gate H in hall 7.1. Each ride follows a secured route of about 25 minutes, with a host in the car explaining what the system does. Places are booked with a QR code on site. France has not approved the system for ordinary owners, but said in September that it will support the approval after testing two cars on public roads. The organiser’s own page quotes two figures from Tesla: more than 100 million kilometres driven in Europe, and a 4.1 times lower probability of having an accident than with manual driving. Those are Tesla’s own figures.

Why it matters: In Norway, Statens vegvesen (SVV), the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, has not allowed Tesla to run customer demos. In May the agency called Tesla’s information material misleading because it did not say the system is driver assistance. As of 3 July SVV had not received updated material. Now driver assistance is in the name itself. That ought to make it easier to allow demos here too. The next chance of an EU yes is TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles) in December 2026. FSD Supervised is SAE Level 2 driver assistance, and the driver is fully responsible. In Norway the system is not yet approved for ordinary owners.

Source: https://teslant.com/en/news/tesla-paris-motor-show-2026-fsd-drives-cybercab

item.title: Christian Democrats in the Storting: Norway gave the EU no input on FSD – Denmark has already said yes
item.description:
Member of parliament Jørgen H. Kristiansen of the Christian Democrats (KrF) has sent a written question about Tesla’s driver assistance system to Transport Minister Kamzy Gunaratnam of the Labour Party (Ap). The question was submitted on 8 October and sent to the minister on 9 October. Kristiansen asks: “Will the government take the initiative to give Norwegian input before the upcoming EU consideration of the driver assistance system Tesla FSD (Supervised), and will the government consider national recognition of the system if it is approved in the EU, as Denmark among others has done?” (our translation). In his reasoning he writes that Statens vegvesen (SVV), the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, has said Norway gave no input to the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV) before the meeting on 6 October. The committee is handling the Dutch case that could give the system approval across the EU. Tesla now calls the system “Tesla Assisted Driving” in Europe. SVV’s own page confirms that Norway sent neither questions nor comments. Denmark has already said yes. The Danish Road Traffic Authority, Færdselsstyrelsen, accepted the provisional approval from RDW, the Dutch approval authority, on 9 June. The authority reviewed the technical documentation and agrees with RDW that the system makes a positive contribution to road safety. Denmark, in other words, did not wait for the EU. The minister replied on 16 October.

Why it matters: Danish Tesla owners with newer hardware (HW4) have been able to use FSD Supervised since June. Eight EU countries, the Netherlands included, have said yes. Norway has no vote in TCMV, but can send input. Before the October meeting Norway chose not to. Nor will SVV go first: the agency is not considering any Norwegian introduction as long as the system does not meet UN Reg. 171 (the UN regulation on driver assistance systems). The next chance of an EU yes is December 2026, and in Norway FSD Supervised is not yet approved for ordinary owners.

Source: https://www.stortinget.no/no/Saker-og-publikasjoner/Sporsmal/Skriftlige-sporsmal-og-svar/Skriftlig-sporsmal/?qnid=127642

item.title: Tesla renames FSD in the Netherlands and other EU countries – the documents show no hidden EU vote
item.description:
Tesla has renamed FSD Supervised on several European websites. On the Dutch page (tesla.com/nl_nl/fsd) the system is now called “Tesla Assisted Driving”. For Germany and Norway we only have screenshots shared on X. They show the name “Tesla Assisted Driving Basic”, in Norwegian “Tesla Assistert kjøring grunnleggende”. According to the German transport ministry (BMV), Tesla itself offered the new name. The German X account @FSD_DE believes the name change and an amended agenda could mean that TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles) did vote on FSD on 6 October after all. That is speculation, not a decision. The agenda was indeed amended on 5 October, the EU’s Comitology Register shows. The meeting was now to end at 12.30 instead of 15.00, two items on heavy vehicles were dropped, and AOB (any other business) was moved to right after the Article 39 item. Article 39 is the exemption procedure the Dutch approval authority RDW used when it approved FSD Supervised in April. The FSD item itself is unchanged, as a continuation of the discussions on the Dutch application, not as a vote. Under the EU comitology regulation (182/2011), member states should as a rule receive the draft of a decision at least 14 days before the meeting. Neither the Commission, RDW nor Tesla has reported any vote, and the minutes have not been published in the register or on CIRCABC. Reuters and Electrek wrote on 8 October that the vote will come in December at the earliest.

Why it matters: The name change removes one of the arguments against FSD. In May Statens vegvesen (SVV), the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, called Tesla’s customer information misleading because it did not say the system is driver assistance. Now it is in the name. The next chance of an EU yes is still December 2026, and in Norway FSD Supervised is not yet approved for ordinary owners.

Source: https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/comitology-register/screen/documents/118164/2/consult

item.title: RDW tested FSD for more than 3,000 hours – Norway’s roads authority dismisses lives saved as “marketing”
item.description:
The Dutch approval authority RDW tested FSD Supervised for more than 3,000 hours and over 1,000 test drives on track and public roads. The conclusion was clear: the system can make traffic safer when used correctly. Even so, Statens vegvesen (SVV), the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, dismisses Tesla’s claims about lives saved as marketing. Chief engineer Stein-Helge Mundal says so in a major review by the news agency Reuters on 7 October – while Norwegian owners are still waiting. Mundal tells Reuters that the agency does not approve systems because they are popular, nor reject them because they are controversial. He also believes the name “Full Self-Driving” can lead drivers to think the car can do more than it can. Reuters has reviewed emails between Tesla and authorities in seven countries, Norway among them. The agency writes that Tesla pushed for a cheaper and less extensive review at RDW, and that seven road safety researchers believe Tesla’s own Europe study does not prove fewer fatal accidents. RDW rejects the criticism: the assessment was independent and thorough, and it recommended approval across the EU. The Czech approval authority says it has no reason to doubt that RDW was impartial. Tesla’s own figures point the same way. According to the safety report for FSD Supervised (tesla.com/fsd/safety), the cars in North America drove an average of about 9.2 million kilometres between each serious collision with the system engaged. Driven manually, with the active safety systems on, cars in the same Tesla fleet managed about 3.3 million kilometres. With FSD they went almost three times as far. The figures cover the past twelve months, and a serious collision means that airbags or other single-use restraints were deployed. Against the average for US cars, Tesla reports seven times fewer serious collisions. The comparison is in line with the yardstick SVV itself uses: in a reply to a Norwegian Tesla enthusiast this summer, Mundal wrote that the car with FSD engaged should be compared with the same car without it (ITavisen, 3 July). Reuters also cites an email from Norwegian Tesla owners in May that called the Norwegian handling passive and bureaucratic.

Why it matters: RDW has done the work: more than 3,000 test hours, a clear safety conclusion and a recommendation of a yes across the EU. Eight EU countries are already running FSD Supervised on that approval. SVV nevertheless is not considering any Norwegian introduction as long as the system does not meet UN Reg. 171 (the UN regulation on driver assistance systems), and the agency has no process of its own with Tesla at present. So Norwegian owners must wait for TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles), where the next chance of a yes is in December. The date is not known. FSD Supervised is SAE Level 2 driver assistance, and the driver is fully responsible.

Source: https://www.reuters.com/investigations/tesla-is-browbeating-eu-approve-its-full-self-driving-tech-pressure-is-working-2026-10-07/

item.title: Slovakia promises an FSD yes “in a few days” – but the letter to the Netherlands has not been sent yet
item.description:
Slovakia’s transport minister Jozef Ráž Jr. says in a video that within a few days Slovakia will send a letter to the Netherlands stating that it recognises the approval of FSD Supervised from RDW, the Dutch approval authority. The system can then be used on Slovak roads. For now this is an announcement, not an approval: we have found no press release from the ministry and no coverage in Slovak media confirming that the letter has been sent. The route is the same one Lithuania, Croatia and the Czech Republic have taken. RDW approved FSD Supervised on 10 April under Article 39, the EU’s exemption procedure for new technology in framework regulation 2018/858. The approval applies only in the Netherlands, but other countries can accept it nationally and notify RDW in writing. That is the letter Ráž is talking about. The Czech Republic did so on 21 September. Since then Slovak owners can use FSD on Czech roads, but the system switches off at the border because the country of registration decides. Until the letter is sent and Tesla confirms a rollout, no Slovak owner can use FSD at home. In the EU the case is at a standstill: the meeting of TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles) on 6 October was discussion only, and the earliest vote is in December. FSD Supervised is SAE Level 2 driver assistance, and the driver is fully responsible.

Why it matters: If Slovakia joins, nine EU countries will be on the Article 39 route, and the pressure ahead of the EU vote grows. Norway is still waiting for Brussels via the EEA, while more and more EU countries take the shortcut themselves. Statens vegvesen, the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, has not approved FSD Supervised for ordinary owners, and a promise in Bratislava is not a decision.

Source: https://x.com/slovakevguy/status/2107848969934274710

item.title: Germany: Bilger pushes for an EU yes – Tesla offers the name TAD and a maximum of ten per cent over the limit
item.description:
The German transport ministry (BMV) updated its status on Tesla’s driver assistance system on 6 October. Minister Steffen Bilger says he wants a swift EU approval of the system, known as FSD Supervised. Tesla has offered to call it “Tesla Assisted Driving” (TAD), because “FSD” is misleading: the system assists, and the driver must pay attention. In September BMV and Tesla agreed that the system may drive at most ten per cent above the speed limit. Germany will support that line constructively in the EU process. The driver remains 100 per cent responsible. BMV is continuing its dialogue with the German Federal Motor Transport Authority KBA (Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt), the Dutch approval authority RDW and Tesla. According to the website heise, citing the news agency dpa, Bilger also said Germany must discuss “what can be done” nationally if the EU route does not succeed. That is political will, not a customer approval. The meeting of TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles) on 6 October was discussion only, with no vote. The earliest EU vote is expected in December. Germany has not opened the system to ordinary customers.

Why it matters: German political pressure for an EU yes could speed up the TCMV route, which Norway depends on through the EEA. The ten per cent cap over the speed limit and the TAD name are concrete compromises in Brussels. There is still no customer approval in Germany or Norway. Eight EU countries have already said yes nationally, and they have about 12.7 per cent of the EU population.

Source: https://www.bmv.de/SharedDocs/DE/Artikel/StV/Digitalisierung-der-Mobilitaet/aktueller-stand-tesla-assistenzsysteme.html

item.title: The TCMV meeting on 6 October has been held – still no vote on FSD Supervised
item.description:
The EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV) met on 6 October. On the agenda was further discussion of the Netherlands’ Article 39 case, that is, the application under the EU exemption procedure in Article 39 of framework regulation 2018/858. There was no vote, as Statens vegvesen (SVV), the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, announced on 2 October. The next chance is December 2026, but the date is not known. When we last checked, only the agenda was in the folder in the EU document archive CIRCABC.

Why it matters: Statens vegvesen has still not approved FSD Supervised for ordinary owners in Norway. Eight EU countries have already said yes nationally, and owners there are driving with the system.

Source: https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/4273d650-b8a9-4093-ac03-18854fbba4b5/library/0f4e0c81-ae0d-445a-80f4-4d9fe3e265c5

item.title: Statens vegvesen: no EU vote on FSD Supervised on 6 October – Norway did not even send questions
item.description:
Statens vegvesen (SVV), the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, confirms that there will be no vote on FSD Supervised when TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles) meets on 6 October. The confirmation is in a new section of the agency’s page on driver assistance systems, “Update 2 October on TCMV meeting”. According to SVV, the reason is that the approval authorities in the majority of member states “have signalled that they are not ready to vote”. “The next opportunity is in December 2026,” the agency writes. Norway has not submitted any questions or comments for the meeting. The “Last updated” field at the bottom of the page still shows 3 July.

Why it matters: Hopes of an EU yes in October are gone, and December is only a possibility. Norway has no vote in TCMV, but can send questions and comments. Before the June meeting Norway was one of few countries that did. This time Norway sent nothing. SVV itself writes that some EU countries have already accepted the exemptions nationally – eight EU countries have said yes to FSD Supervised. Even so, the agency will not go first. SVV is “not considering any earlier introduction of the system in Norway” as long as it does not meet UN Reg. 171 (the UN regulation on driver assistance systems, DCAS), and has “no process with Tesla on this at present”. Norwegian owners must wait for the EU decision and then for SVV to continue the process under the EEA Agreement.

Source: https://www.vegvesen.no/fag/trafikk/its-portalen/its-i-statens-vegvesen/metr/forerstottesystemer/

item.title: Croatia becomes the eighth EU country with FSD Supervised – Norway is still left out
item.description:
Croatia has approved FSD Supervised, according to Tesla Europe. “FSD Supervised now approved in Croatia,” the company’s official X account @teslaeurope wrote at 10.02 on Tuesday 29 September 2026. The rollout starts soon, Tesla promises. That makes eight EU countries that have said yes to the system, covering about 12.7 per cent of the EU population (Eurostat, 1 January 2025). We have not yet found a separate announcement from the Croatian transport ministry (MMPI). The date of the decision and any conditions are therefore not confirmed.

Why it matters: Yet another EU country says yes while Norwegian owners wait. Statens vegvesen, the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, has not approved FSD Supervised for ordinary owners, and as an EEA country Norway has no vote in TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles). The agenda for the 6 October meeting still has no vote, and the press points to December as the earliest chance. Eight countries and 12.7 per cent are a long way from the thresholds of 15 countries and 65 per cent of the population.

Source: https://x.com/teslaeurope

item.title: EU vote in December at the earliest: the agenda for 6 October has only further discussion
item.description:
The EU vote on Tesla’s FSD Supervised will come in December at the earliest, Reuters and TeslaNorth reported on 25 September 2026. The agenda for the meeting of TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles) on 6 October points the same way. It is in the EU document archive CIRCABC. There the Netherlands’ Article 39 case is listed as a “continuation of discussions”, not a vote. Article 39 is the EU exemption procedure in framework regulation 2018/858 that lets one country approve new technology before the EU has common rules. The dispute over how far the system may drive above the speed limit (Speed Offset) and resistance from Nordic countries have pushed the vote back. Even so, the system is already in use in seven EU countries.

Why it matters: According to the press and the agenda, the chance of a vote in October is gone. December is the earliest the press expects. Norwegian owners have no approval, and there is no set Norwegian date.

item.title: CIRCABC agenda for TCMV on 6 October: the Article 39 case will be discussed further, ADS rules under any other business
item.description:
The draft agenda for the 119th meeting of TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles) is dated Brussels, 11 September 2026. The meeting will be held on 6 October 2026 from 10.00 to 15.00. The agenda is in the EU document archive CIRCABC. From 11.45 to 12.10 it lists “Continuation of discussions on request of the Netherlands for an Art. 39 authorisation”. Article 39 is the EU exemption procedure for new technology in framework regulation 2018/858. No vote is planned. Under AOB (any other business) from 14.30 to 15.00 it lists “Updates on the preparation of secondary legislation for large-series ADS and alignment with AI Act”. That is a briefing on the work on supplementary rules for large-series automated driving systems (ADS) and on alignment with the EU AI Act. That item is not a vote either.

Why it matters: The document text in CIRCABC now confirms the meeting date and that both the Article 39 case and ADS are on the agenda. A vote is still not listed. Norwegian owners have no approval, while seven EU countries are already driving with FSD Supervised.

Source: https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/4273d650-b8a9-4093-ac03-18854fbba4b5/library/0f4e0c81-ae0d-445a-80f4-4d9fe3e265c5?p=1&n=10&sort=modified_DESC

item.title: Johanna.be: FSD Supervised exceeded the 30 limit in 55% of tests in Brussels
item.description:
The Belgian voluntary organisation Johanna.be tested FSD Supervised over about 400 kilometres in Brussels in July. According to Electrek and Reuters, as cited by IEX on 24 September, the car drove too fast on 55 per cent of the stretches with a 30 limit, at an average of 44 km/h. On stretches with a 20 limit the share was 42 per cent. The screen often showed 50 where the sign said 30. The report has been sent to RDW, the Dutch type-approval authority. RDW told Reuters it will consider the report as part of its ongoing monitoring and supervision of the system. That does not mean the approval is being withdrawn, and the case is not formally reopened. The debate over how far the system may drive above the speed limit (Speed Offset) comes just before the meeting of TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles). According to Reuters, Tesla points to its own data: 4.1 times fewer collisions with FSD than with manual driving, measured over more than 100 million kilometres.

Why it matters: The test feeds into the speed debate that Statens vegvesen (SVV), the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, has already highlighted. Norwegian owners have no approval, while seven EU countries are already driving with the system. The agenda in the EU document archive CIRCABC confirms the meeting on 6 October. There the Netherlands’ Article 39 case is listed as further discussion, not a vote.

item.title: Latvia’s economics ministry proposes that the government recognise the Dutch approval of FSD Supervised
item.description:
On 21 September 2026 Latvia’s Ministry of Economics published a proposal for the government to recognise the type-approval from RDW, the Dutch approval authority. RDW granted the approval under the EU exemption procedure in Article 39 of framework regulation 2018/858. If the government says yes, the Latvian Road Traffic Safety Directorate CSDD will have ten working days to complete Tesla’s application. This is not yet a customer approval: Latvia has no national approval until the decision has been made.

Why it matters: It is a formal follow-up in the Baltics after Estonia and Lithuania, but for now only a proposal. It does not change the count of yes countries in TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles). The status is uncertain until the government has adopted the recognition.

Source: https://en.bb.lv/article/technologies/2026/09/21/in-latvia-teslas-next-generation-autopilot-may-be-allowed-110761

item.title: The Czech Republic becomes a yes country on the TCMV map: 7 of 27 countries and 11.8% of the population
item.description:
On 21 September 2026 the Czech transport ministry recognised the Netherlands’ Article 39 case, that is, the approval under the EU exemption procedure in Article 39 of framework regulation 2018/858. The same day Latvia’s Ministry of Economics proposed that the government recognise the approval. That is still uncertain, and it is not a customer approval. Our unofficial estimate for a yes in TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles) in October is set at 30 per cent.

Why it matters: The arithmetic improved slightly, but the thresholds of 15 countries and 65 per cent of the population still require the large countries to join.

item.title: The Czech Republic becomes the seventh EU country with national recognition of FSD Supervised
item.description:
On 21 September 2026 the Czech transport ministry recognised the type-approval the Netherlands granted Tesla FSD Supervised under Article 39, the EU exemption procedure in framework regulation 2018/858. Tesla Europe confirms that the rollout is coming soon. The seven countries now cover about 11.8 per cent of the EU population. Norwegian owners still have no approval.

Why it matters: It adds population weight ahead of the meeting of TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles) on 6 October, which is on the agenda in the EU document archive CIRCABC. Even so, it is far below the thresholds of 15 countries and 65 per cent of the population. Statens vegvesen, the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, has not changed its line for Norway.

item.title: Slovenia becomes the sixth EU country with national customer approval
item.description:
Tesla Europe says Slovenia has recognised the Netherlands’ Article 39 case, that is, the approval under the EU exemption procedure in Article 39 of framework regulation 2018/858. The rollout is expected soon. Even so, the six countries cover only about 9.4 per cent of the EU population.

Why it matters: That is still far below the thresholds for a yes in TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles): 15 of 27 countries and 65 per cent of the population.

item.title: France starts UTAC road tests after a conversation between Musk and Tabarot
item.description:
French transport minister Philippe Tabarot says he had a constructive conversation with Elon Musk on 2 September. Tesla provided two production cars with FSD Supervised for independent road tests at UTAC, the French testing and certification body. Reuters reports on the tests. This is not a French customer approval.

That the country is testing after its no in July is a clear sign of a thaw, but it is still not an approval.

item.title: Sweden repeats that the goal is an EU-wide approval of FSD Supervised
item.description:
In a written answer to the Riksdag, Sweden’s parliament, on 31 August 2026, Infrastructure Minister Andreas Carlson says the ambition is an approval that applies across the EU, after evaluations. He did not promise that Sweden will vote yes.

Why it matters: It is an official Swedish signal ahead of the meeting of TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles): Sweden wants an approval in the EU if the safety case holds up.

item.title: Sweden’s infrastructure minister filmed in a Tesla with FSD in Mullsjö
item.description:
Around 30 August 2026, Infrastructure Minister Andreas Carlson posted an Instagram story from approved FSD testing in Mullsjö. It is not a Swedish approval for ordinary owners.

Why it matters: It shows political interest in the system in Sweden, but it is a symbol and not a green light for Swedish owners.

item.title: Statens vegvesen’s page was last updated on 3 July 2026
item.description:
Statens vegvesen (SVV), the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, repeats that FSD Supervised is not approved for customers in Norway. Only limited testing is allowed. Customer demos are on hold until Tesla changes its messaging. The next chance in TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles) was then expected in October.

Why it matters: This is the official Norwegian line until SVV publishes a newer update.

Source: https://www.vegvesen.no/fag/trafikk/its-portalen/its-i-statens-vegvesen/metr/forerstottesystemer/

item.title: TCMV discusses the Netherlands’ Article 39 case – no vote
item.description:
TCMV (the EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles) discussed the Netherlands’ application under Article 39, the EU exemption procedure in framework regulation 2018/858, on 30 June 2026. There was no vote. Norway took part without voting rights.

Why it matters: The first realistic chance of a vote was then expected in the autumn. The EU document archive CIRCABC confirms a meeting on 6 October, but not necessarily a vote.
